title: Update: 12 pre-registered crypto strategies, 0 survivors. What I did in 3 weeks with your feedback, and where I'm stuck now
author: worldrecchicken
selftext:
Three weeks ago I posted that none of my 12 pre-registered BTC/ETH spot strategies survived costs and placebo tests. I got a lot of good replies, so here's the promised update. Still paper money only, still spot only, long only. No leverage, no borrowing, no derivatives (hard personal rule, not up for discussion).

Short version: still nothing survives. But the testing got better, and I now know a lot better what I don't know.

First, a correction

In my first post I said I'm collecting liquidation data. That was wrong. I collect order book snapshots, cross-exchange lead-lag, news, scheduled events (FOMC etc.) and since Oct 19 also macro (DXY, US rates, S&P 500, Nasdaq 100, gold) hourly. No liquidations. Sorry to the people who replied on that basis.

What I did

1. Replayed my live "sandbox" strategies on 7 years of history

The paper bot runs 48 simple rules (breakouts, dips, momentum, RSI, Bollinger, hourly variants with filters). I replayed all of them on 2019–2026 with costs (0.10%/side + slippage), next-candle fills, and a placebo entry with the same exit profile.

\- BTC/ETH: 0 of 64 strategy×market combos net positive. Best was "4h momentum, strong" at −0.12%/trade. Placebo was −0.25%/trade, so it is better than random, just not better than zero.

\- SOL/XRP: 0 of 86 net positive. Best −0.07%/trade, placebo −0.26 / −0.28%.

\- The hourly-candle rules: all 8 indistinguishable from their hourly placebo, all negative.

So some rules beat a random entry, but none beat the costs. That pattern was the same on all four coins.

2. Maker fees don't save it

Someone suggested limit orders. On my venue maker is 0.08% vs taker 0.10%, so the best case saving is 0.04% per round trip. My best rule is −0.12%/trade. Even with perfect maker fills it stays negative, and as several of you said, maker fills tend to come exactly when price moves against you. I dropped that route.

3. My "48 strategies" are not 48 bets

I measured overlap. In the first week of live paper trading there were 1,806 sandbox entries but only 310 distinct market-hours. On average \~2.1–2.2 strategies per independent bet. The whole breakout family (1h/4h/12h/24h + 3 mixes) was 100% identical in entries. So my effective number of tests is much lower than 48, and one market move can tick a lot of boxes at once (same lesson as the 10/10 night).

4. Sequential futility testing

The sandbox needs hundreds to thousands of trades per strategy before I can judge anything (deadline July 2027). To stop wasting time on hopeless rules, I pre-registered a futility check with an e-process (e-values, Bonferroni over strategies). It can only declare a rule hopeless earlier, never declare it proven earlier.

5. Plumbing problems I found in my own bot

The paper bot's main loop sometimes lagged up to 2.4 s, giving \~800 latency errors in two weeks and about 9 signals rejected because data was too old. Fixed on Oct 28, now measuring before vs after. Lesson: paper trading measures your infrastructure too, not just your strategy.



Where I'm stuck. These are the questions I'd really like deep answers on:

1. Multiple testing with heavily correlated strategies

48 rules, \~2 rules per independent bet, clusters that are 100% identical. Bonferroni over 48 is far too strict, over "families" feels hand-wavy. Would you use Romano-Wolf stepdown, White's Reality Check / Hansen's SPA, or estimate an effective number of tests from the overlap? And how do you combine that with sequential testing over time?

2. Defining an "independent episode"

Trades overlap in time and across strategies. What's a defensible rule? Merge entries within X hours on the same market? Cluster by drawdown/recovery cycles? Something based on the autocorrelation of returns? I want to fix this before I see the next results, not after.

3. Power, honestly

With 0.20% round-trip friction and the sample sizes I can reach by mid-2027, what effect size can I realistically detect? I'll compute a minimum detectable effect per rule, but if you've done this for short-horizon crypto: what's typical? I'd rather hear "your setup can never see an edge under X bps" now than in a year.

4. My last attempt (1 of 13 left)

Most of you pointed the same way: forced flows, not price patterns. Liquidation cascades, index/fund rebalancing on known dates, funding resets. The most concrete idea from the thread: buy spot after a liquidation wave is over (open interest stops falling, funding normalizes), hold a fixed window, compare against random entries with the same hold time.

\- How do you define "the wave is over" using only data up to t, without it quietly becoming "price stopped falling"?

\- On spot only, does this survive 0.20% round trip at multi-day holds, or does it mostly exist on perps?

\- Any documented retail-reachable flow with a known calendar (rebalances, unlocks, ETF flows) that you'd pick over liquidations?

5. Paper vs live

I fill at the next price + slippage and assume full fills at €500 per trade. What did you see going live at small size on BTC/ETH: partial fills, queue position, latency? What would you add to a paper model before trusting it?

What's running now

Paper bot 24/7 on real OKX prices. 48 sandbox rules on BTC/ETH and 48 on SOL/XRP (always kept separate, never summed), each with a pre-set trade count and deadline. First evaluation moment is mid-December. Next update then, pass or fail.



Thanks again. The replies in the last thread changed the test more than anything I read elsewhere.
